The Lighthouse Keepers

For most of two centuries the lights along the coast were kept by families who lived beside them. The work was the same every night: trim the wicks, polish the lenses, wind the clockwork that turned the beam, and write down the weather in a log that nobody but the inspector would ever read.

Electrification arrived slowly and then all at once. A keeper who had climbed the same stairs for thirty years could be replaced by a timer and a fortnightly visit, and by the end of the century almost every light on the coast was running on its own, watched from a control room many miles away.
